title: Attenuated node heartbeat caused silent eviction and cascading fallback surge
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Summary:
On 2025-02-10 at ~03:12 UTC a subtle change in the regional aggregator's heartbeat filtering caused a set of healthy GPU hosts in us-west-2 to be temporarily deprioritized. The control plane interpreted attenuated heartbeat metrics as node degradation, triggering an automated drain and a cascade of tier fallbacks. Client requests were routed to fallback variants (higher-latency and higher-cost) and to more distant regions, increasing median tail latency by ~220ms and pushing per-token costs up ~48% for affected customers for a 38-minute window.

Detection:
- Pager alert triggered at 03:18 UTC: elevated fallback-rate on us-west-2 (alert threshold: fallback_rate > 5% over 5m).
- On-call (SRE) investigated routing metrics and found rapid node-weight drops in the regional aggregator feed.
- Initial dashboard showed no CPU/GPU load spike or infra OOMs on the affected hosts.

Timeline (all times UTC):
- 03:10: config rollout (routing-aggregator v2.7.1) begins; change included histogram bucketing tweak to compress heartbeat noise.
- 03:12: aggregator starts emitting attenuated heartbeat scores for ~22 hosts in us-west-2 (sustained for ~4m).
- 03:15: control plane marks 18 hosts as draining; routing layer begins failing over to tier-B and fallback variants.
- 03:18: automated alert fires; SRE paged.
- 03:22: emergency rollback of aggregator config to v2.7.0 initiated.
- 03:26: node weights recover; draining canceled; traffic gradually shifts back.
- 03:48: fallbacks subsided and metrics returned to baseline.

Root cause analysis:
- The 2.7.1 change adjusted histogram bucket boundaries to reduce heartbeat jitter in normal conditions. Under the operational heartbeat distribution for us-west-2 (more short-lived spot-backed hosts), the new buckets caused a disproportionate number of heartbeats to be aggregated into a low-weight bucket. The weight-transformation function treated the low bucket as a signal for degradation rather than noise.
- There was no upstream resource failure; hosts were healthy. The misclassification came from an interaction between the new bucket boundaries and our weight-synthesis rule (weight < 0.2 => drain candidate).
- The control plane lacks a short-lived hysteresis for decommission signals derived from aggregator buckets: a single 4-minute attenuation was sufficient to trigger drain decisions.

Mitigations performed during incident:
- Rollback of aggregator config to v2.7.0 (03:22 UTC) — immediate recovery of heartbeat scores.
- Temporary adjustment of drain threshold to require 2 consecutive low-weight windows (5m windows) for decommission (emergency override) while root cause was investigated.
- Increased autoscaling headroom in west region to absorb transient reroutes.

Impact details:
- Affected customers: four production tenants with high rps in us-west-2.
- User-visible: increased 95th/99th latencies and degraded SLO for 38 minutes. No request failures or data loss.
- Cost: temporary uplift due to routing to higher-cost variants and cross-region egress; estimated incremental charge: ~$12k across high-usage tenants for the window.

Postmortem conclusions and learning:
- Small heuristic changes in aggregator summarization can have outsized impacts on downstream routing logic. Bucketing changes must be evaluated against the full distribution of heartbeat patterns across regions and instance types.
- The control plane needs stronger short-lived hysteresis and a quorum mechanism before initiating decommission/drain flows.
- Observability gap: the aggregator emitted bucket-level metrics, but we didn't have a simple end-to-end visualization that correlated bucket shifts to drain decisions in real time.

Permanent corrective actions (see action_items for owners):
1) Revert the histogram bucketing change in the long-term branch; replace with an adaptive smoothing algorithm tested across regional distributions.
2) Add a hysteresis layer in the decommission decision path: require N consecutive low-weight windows OR corroborating signals (e.g., host health + ingress latency) before draining.
3) Introduce a "quorum check" where at least 3 independent signals must indicate degradation for region-scale drains.
4) Add an end-to-end routing-debug dashboard that overlays aggregator bucket/time-series, control-plane decisions, and active rollouts.
5) Expand canary testing: apply aggregator summarization changes first to low-traffic regions and observed spot-backed host mixes with chaos tests (simulated heartbeat attenuation).
6) Update runbooks: clearer rollback steps, stair-step thresholds for emergency override, and explicit cost impact estimation.

Validation and rollout plan:
- Implement fixes in a feature branch and run region-mirroring load tests with synthetic heartbeat distributions that match us-west-2.
- Deploy to canary region (eu-west-1) with 2h observation window and automated guardrails (cancellation if fallback_rate > 1% for 5m).
- If stable, staged rollout to remaining regions over 48h with hourly gating.

Communications:
- Customer notifications: outreach to the four affected tenants was performed by Customer Success with incident summary and cost impact by 2025-02-11 16:00 UTC.
- Public status page: minor degraded performance message posted during incident window; cleared after metrics returned to baseline.

References:

- Incident runbook used: https://confluence.redwood.ai/incidents/runbooks/routing-drain.md
- Monitoring dashboard (internal): https://metrics.redwood.ai/dashboards/routing/agg-buckets
